claims.text: The target Mg-containing lightweight HEAs have densities below 6 g/cm³.
The initial induction-melted alloy is in a non-equilibrium or metastable state.
The initial microstructure contains a mixture of solid-solution regions and metastable phases.
Thermal annealing at 400–600°C for sufficient time promotes phase transformation.
During thermal exposure, metastable solid-solution regions preferentially transform into stable intermetallic compounds.
Sufficient Mg content promotes intermetallic formation.
Thermal exposure drives diffusion and nucleation of intermetallic compounds.
Formation of the intermetallic compounds reduces compositional heterogeneity.
The resulting intermetallic compounds act as corrosion barriers.
The intermetallic compounds form microstructurally connected pathways that enable rapid high-temperature oxidation.
The resulting intermetallic compounds have lower oxidation resistance than the initial metastable structure.
Annealing will lower the corrosion rate relative to the as-cast non-equilibrium baseline.
Annealing will increase high-temperature oxidation mass gain or oxide-scale growth relative to the as-cast non-equilibrium baseline.
The predicted behavior does not apply to fully equilibrated or single-phase alloys.
The effects may be weaker when intermetallic compounds are discontinuous.
The effects may be weaker when protective oxide films form.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes decomposition of solid-solution regions into distinct intermetallic compounds while also asserting that this reduces compositional heterogeneity; without a homogenization pathway, intermetallic precipitation would commonly create or preserve chemical partitioning rather than necessarily reduce it.
